issues.legal_issue: A completed public-auction sale cannot be set aside solely because nonparticipants later offer more or property values subsequently rise, absent concrete proof of a defect that vitiated the auction or made the sale price wholly inadequate.
material_facts: The property was sold through a public auction conducted after the prescribed procedure, with 45 participants.
The successful bidder’s offer substantially exceeded the announced expected price, and the sale was confirmed by the competent authority after a report from the Assistant Commissioner.
The full consideration was paid, a sale deed was executed, and possession was delivered.
The challengers had not participated in the auction; one later offered a higher price but did not deposit the money, and the other made a later offer.
No court or authority found the auction illegal or irregular, and no concrete material established fraud, collusion, or that the property had been sold at a throwaway price.
The High Court ordered a re-auction more than two decades after the sale, relying on later offers and an inference about the property’s value.
issues.conclusion: The direction for a re-auction was set aside because later offers and an unsupported inference of undervaluation did not justify disturbing the completed sale; concrete proof of fraud, collusion, material irregularity or illegality, or a throwaway sale price was absent.
issues.legal_principle: A public-auction sale to the highest bidder, once confirmed and completed, should not be disturbed on the basis of subsequent offers by nonparticipants. There must be concrete material establishing a vitiating ground, such as fraud, collusion, material irregularity or illegality, or a throwaway price. The Court relied on the locus and writ-jurisdiction principles in Jasbhai Motibhai Desai v. Roshan Kumar, Haji Bashir Ahmed (1976) 1 SCC 671, and on the cautions against non-genuine public-interest litigation in State of Uttaranchal v. Balwant Singh Chaufal (2010) 3 SCC 402. It acknowledged the general principles concerning obtaining the best price in public sales discussed in Navalkha and Sons v. Sri Ramanya Das (1969) 3 SCC 537, Divya Manufacturing Company (P) Ltd. v. Union Bank of India (2000) 6 SCC 69, Chairman and Managing Director, SIPCOT v. Contromix Pvt. Ltd. (1995) 4 SCC 595, and Union Bank of India v. Official Liquidator (2000) 5 SCC 274, but held that they did not assist the challengers on these facts.

rule.if: completed_public_auction_challenge and auction_followed_required_process and sale_confirmed_and_completed and challenger_did_not_participate and no_proven_vitiating_defect and challenge_relies_on_later_offer_or_price_inference

predicates.completed_public_auction_challenge: The proceeding challenges a sale completed through a public auction.
predicates.auction_followed_required_process: The authority conducted the auction after following the applicable procedure.
predicates.sale_confirmed_and_completed: The competent authority confirmed the sale and the purchaser completed payment and obtained a sale deed or possession.
predicates.challenger_did_not_participate: The person challenging the sale did not participate in the auction or submit a bid.
predicates.no_proven_vitiating_defect: The record does not concretely establish fraud, collusion, material irregularity or illegality, or a throwaway sale price.
predicates.challenge_relies_on_later_offer_or_price: The challenge relies on a later offer or an unsupported inference that the property was worth more than the auction price.

issues.definition: When a completed public-auction sale is challenged by a nonparticipant and the challenge rests on a later offer or unsupported price inference without a proven defect that vitiated the sale, the sale is not set aside on that basis.

issues.legal_issue: A nonparticipant without an individual legal interest cannot use a public-interest challenge to upset a public auction, and a successor cannot continue a proceeding that was brought as public-interest litigation.
material_facts: The original challenger did not participate in the auction or submit an offer.
The auction had attracted numerous participants, and the challenger had no individual interest in the auctioned property identified in the record.

The challenger pursued the matter as a public-interest litigation, but the Court found the proceeding to be a private-interest challenge in the guise of a public cause and found no established auction irregularity or illegality.
After the original challenger died, his wife sought to continue the proceedings.
issues.conclusion: The original challenger lacked standing to challenge the auction in these circumstances, and his wife could not continue the public-interest litigation as his heir.
issues.legal_principle: Ordinarily, a person invoking the extraordinary writ jurisdiction must show infringement of a legal right or prejudice to a legal interest; strangers and busybodies without a genuine interest should not be permitted to interfere. The Court relied on Jasbhai Motibhai Desai v. Roshan Kumar, Haji Bashir Ahmed (1976) 1 SCC 671, and applied the safeguards for genuine public-interest litigation stated in State of Uttaranchal v. Balwant Singh Chaufal (2010) 3 SCC 402, including scrutiny of the petitioner’s credentials, the existence of substantial public interest, and the absence of private or oblique motives.

predicates.public_law_challenge_to_auction: The proceeding invokes public-law jurisdiction to challenge a public auction.
predicates.challenger_is_nonparticipant_stranger: The person who initiated the challenge neither participated in the auction nor submitted a bid.
predicates.challenger_lacks_individual_legal_intere: The challenger has no individual legal right or interest in the property or auction identified as the basis for the challenge.
predicates.claimant_is_successor_to_pil_filer: The person seeking to continue the proceeding is the successor or heir of the person who initiated it.
predicates.proceeding_is_public_interest_litigation: The proceeding was brought as public-interest litigation rather than as a claim based on the claimant’s own legal right.

issues.definition: A nonparticipant stranger without an individual legal interest lacks standing to challenge the auction through public-law proceedings, and a successor lacks standing to continue a proceeding brought as public-interest litigation.

issues.legal_issue: The relevant property value for assessing whether a public-auction sale was inadequate is its value when the auction was conducted, not its value after substantial time has passed.
material_facts: The auction and sale occurred more than two decades before the High Court ordered a re-auction.
The respondents relied on the property’s much higher value at the time of the later proceedings.
They identified no material showing that the successful bid was below the property’s fair value when the auction took place.
The successful bid exceeded the announced base price, and numerous people participated in the auction.
issues.conclusion: Later appreciation in the property’s value did not justify a re-auction; the relevant inquiry was the property’s value at the time of the original auction, and no material established that the price then was unfair.
issues.legal_principle: In assessing whether an auction price was inadequate, the relevant value is the value at the time of the auction, not a value reached after the passage of years. In the absence of allegations and proof of fraud, collusion, cartel conduct, or another material irregularity or illegality, the highest offer in a competitive public auction may be accepted as fair value.

predicates.public_auction_price_adequacy_challenge: The proceeding disputes whether the price obtained at a public auction was adequate.
predicates.later_property_appreciation_is_relied_on: The challenger relies on an increase in the property’s value after the auction.
predicates.no_concrete_evidence_of_inadequate_value: The record contains no concrete material showing that the auction price was inadequate when the auction occurred.

issues.definition: When a price-adequacy challenge relies on later appreciation but lacks concrete evidence of inadequacy at the auction, adequacy is assessed by the property’s value at the auction, not its later value.

issues.legal_issue: A public trust that conducted and completed an auction sale, and did not challenge that sale before the successful bidder obtained relief, cannot later challenge its own decision in the circumstances of this case.
material_facts: The Temple’s Executive Officer conducted the auction, obtained the required clearance, and executed the sale deed in favour of the successful bidder.
The Temple did not challenge the auction or sale on the ground of inadequate consideration before the Single Judge ruled in favour of the purchaser.
The Temple then appealed against that judgment without establishing fraud or collusion in the sale.
issues.conclusion: The Temple’s appeal against its own completed auction and sale should not have been entertained in these circumstances.
issues.legal_principle: The Court held that the Temple could not challenge its own decision after its Executive Officer had conducted the auction, obtained the clearance, and executed the sale deed, when the Temple had not previously challenged the sale as inadequate. The Court also noted the absence of allegations of fraud or collusion against the Temple.

rule.if: appeal_by_public_trust_against_judgment_upholding_auction and trust_conducted_auction_and_executed_sale and trust_did_not_previously_challenge_sale and no_proven_fraud_or_collusion

predicates.appeal_by_public_trust_against_judgment_: A public trust appeals from a judgment that upheld a completed auction sale.
predicates.trust_conducted_auction_and_executed_sal: The trust’s officer conducted the auction and executed the sale documents for the purchaser.
predicates.trust_did_not_previously_challenge_sale: The trust did not challenge the sale as inadequate before the purchaser obtained a favourable judgment.
predicates.no_proven_fraud_or_collusion: The record does not establish fraud or collusion in the auction or sale.

issues.definition: When a public trust conducted and completed an auction sale and did not previously challenge it, the trust cannot later challenge its own sale in an appeal absent proven fraud or collusion.
